newsitem.title: ITALY: Battery car left for dead by hybrids, fuel cells.
newsitem.headline: Battery car left for dead by hybrids, fuel cells.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
The battery is being left on the starting blocks as the automobile industry rushes to develop new technologies to replace scarce and polluting fossil fuels, experts told a conference Wednesday.
The inside track will shortly be held by hybrid engines, which combine diesel or petrol power with an electric motor.

The fuel cell is the vision of the future, with cars propelled by electric motors fueled by hydrogen derived from a range of sources including renewable fuels like ethanol. Natural gas, which experts reckon will still be available some 20 years after oil supplies run out by about 2040, is expected to the major provider of hydrogen power. Propane and gasoline will also have a role to play.

And of course fusion power, which one day may produce almost limitless, pollution-free power by mimicing the action of the sun, is part of the nirvana sc enario, where all energy is renewable with other sources like hydroelectric, wind and solar.

Japan's biggest car company, Toyota Motor Corp, recently rocked the competition by announcing that it will introduce a hybrid gasoline-electric powered car on to the local market by the end of this year.

This leapfrogs the competition like Honda Motor Co and General Motors Corp, which are most prominent in offering battery powered vehicles. These so-called zero emission vehicles do not pollute where they are used, but of course need to suck power from conventional power stations.
The Honda and GM electric vehicles suffer from the traditional ailments of the battery. Inconveniently low range, high cost, and poor overall performance.

The Toyota vehicle offers twice the fuel economy of conventional gasoline vehicles. It claims 79 miles per gallon, and massive reduction in emissions of carbon dioxide, and oxides of nitrogen. When the engine is working in its internal combustion phase it powers th e battery, as well, which cuts in when the car approaches city centres.
